Is there any reason to suspect the existence of a foundation of history under the superstructure of legend? Here’s a brief summary of some of the evidence for the historicity of Homer’s works . I’ll write ‘Homer’ as a shorthand for whoever put the poems into the form in which they were written down, some time in the 8th century BCE, without taking a position on exactly how this happened.

Troy was destroyed and its location lost, but when it was rediscovered by Frank Calvert and Heinrich Schliemann in the late 19th century it was where Homer had described it.

Homer describes a Greece in which the major powers included Agamemnon’s Mycenae, Nestor’s Pylos, and Idomeneus’ Knossos. By the classical period these were places of little account compared to Sparta and Athens. Nonetheless, archaeologists have confirmed Homer’s account by finding rich Bronze Age palace complexes at all three sites.

Homer describes equipment and tactics that must have been unfamiliar at the time the poems were written down. For example, in the Iliad the Achaeans and the Trojans have chariots, although these disappeared from Greece after the end of the Mycenaean period. And the combatants have shields that are described as ‘circular’ (like the shields of classical Greece) but which nonetheless cover the warrior’s whole body. Archaeological finds from the Mycenaean period have revealed that Mycenaeans put much store in chariots, and had large shields of rectangular or figure-of-eight shape, for example as depicted on the ‘Lion Hunt’ dagger :

Homer uses grammatical forms that had died out of Greek by the time that the poems were composed, such as the -oio ending in the genitive case (which had become -ou by Homer’s time). This suggests that Homer’s works draw on a long-standing oral tradition. The decipherment of Linear B tablets confirms that these grammatical forms were in use in the Mycenaean period.

Her campaign platform also includes calls for better mobile coverage along the Stuart Highway corridor and mandatory consultation with traditional owners on all mining applications affecting sacred sites.

Asked whether standing as an independent invites accusations of wasting votes or splitting preferences, Jennings laughed softly. “Every serious change starts with someone deciding they won’t wait for permission from head office,” she replied. “If I earn even ten percent first preference support and force the majors to address our concerns, that’s already success.” Recent polling suggests independents could attract up to fifteen percent in some booths across Daly, though experts caution sample sizes are small.

Her background differs sharply from typical political aspirants. Before moving north twelve years ago, Jennings worked as a secondary school science teacher in Victoria. A mother of two adult sons, she lists birdwatching and restoring native vegetation among hobbies when time allows between door-knocking sessions. Campaign finances come solely from donations capped at five hundred dollars per individual donor — another point of pride.

Critics note she lacks legislative experience compared with opponents like Venes, a former union organiser, or Civitarese, whose family name remains well-known locally through business ties dating back decades. Jennings acknowledges this gap openly. “What I lack in parliamentary procedure books,” she admits without hesitation toward cynicism often aimed at outsiders, “I make up for knowing how things actually work around kitchen tables where decisions really happen.”
